cards.definition: Glucagon is secreted by pancreatic alpha cells and promotes hepatic glucose output, including glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, helping maintain glucose availability between meals. This is not a claim that glucagon directly reverses every insulin action in every tissue, nor that it directly drives skeletal-muscle glycogen breakdown in the same way.
required_concepts: Glucagon is a pancreatic alpha-cell hormone.
It promotes hepatic glucose output through glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the appropriate physiological context.
accepted_variants: Alpha-cell glucagon signals the liver to mobilize and produce glucose; it is not insulin's exact inverse in every tissue.
major_error_concepts: Calling glucagon a beta-cell hormone that principally suppresses liver glucose production.
Assuming glucagon directly produces the opposite of every insulin effect in every cell.

cards.prompt: What is Glucose Homeostasis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Glucose homeostasis balances production, absorption, uptake, storage, and use across tissues. Hormonal and neural signals coordinate these fluxes, so a stable concentration can conceal substantial ongoing turnover.
required_concepts: Multiple fluxes maintain a regulated glucose pool.
major_error_concepts: Inferring no glucose production or use from a stable blood concentration.

cards.prompt: What is Calcium Regulation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Calcium regulation coordinates intestinal uptake, skeletal exchange, and renal handling through hormonal and local mechanisms. Extracellular calcium concentration and total skeletal calcium stores are related but not identical quantities.
required_concepts: Several organs regulate a small circulating pool and larger stores.
major_error_concepts: Equating one extracellular calcium concentration with total body calcium content.

cards.prompt: What is Water and Electrolyte Balance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Water and electrolyte balance integrates intake, distribution, transport, and losses across compartments. Osmotic concentration, circulating volume, and total body stores are distinct variables that can change differently.
required_concepts: Concentration, volume, and total content require separate accounting.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a normal concentration guarantees normal total volume and total solute stores.

cards.prompt: What is Energy Expenditure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Energy expenditure is the rate of energy use across maintenance, activity, and other biological processes. It differs from energy intake or stored energy, and its measurement depends on timescale and accounting assumptions.
required_concepts: Energy-use rate differs from intake and storage.
major_error_concepts: Equating food energy consumed with energy expended over the same short interval.

cards.prompt: What is Basal Metabolic Rate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Basal metabolic rate is energy expenditure measured under specified baseline conditions intended to minimize activity and recent feeding effects. It is an operational measure rather than a universal constant independent of body state and measurement conditions.
required_concepts: A standardized baseline measure requires defined conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating any resting measurement after activity or eating as automatically identical to basal metabolic rate.

cards.prompt: What is Heat Transfer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Body heat exchange occurs through radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation under relevant environmental conditions. Net direction depends on gradients, and evaporation can remove heat even when ambient temperature limits other routes.
required_concepts: Distinct physical pathways transfer heat according to conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all heat-transfer routes always move heat outward regardless of surroundings.

cards.prompt: What is Thermoregulatory Effectors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Thermoregulatory effectors alter heat production, heat transfer, or behavior to regulate body temperature. Responses can trade off water, energy, and circulatory demands, so temperature control is integrated with other physiological needs.
required_concepts: Multiple effectors balance thermal control with other resource demands.
major_error_concepts: Assuming maximal sweating or maximal heat production is always optimal in every environment.

cards.prompt: What is Exercise Integration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Exercise physiology examines coordinated responses to increased activity demands, including muscle, circulation, ventilation, and fuel use. Acute responses differ from longer-term adaptation, and one measurement does not specify the capacity of every system.
required_concepts: Activity demand elicits coordinated acute and adaptive responses.
major_error_concepts: Equating a single heart-rate value with a complete measure of all exercise capacity.

cards.prompt: What is Oxygen Consumption? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Oxygen consumption is the rate at which oxygen is taken up and used over a defined system boundary. It informs aerobic metabolism under appropriate assumptions but does not directly measure all nonoxidative energy contributions.
required_concepts: Oxygen-use rate captures a defined aspect of metabolic activity.
major_error_concepts: Assuming oxygen consumption alone quantifies every energy pathway without assumptions.

cards.prompt: What is Fick Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Fick principle relates organ or whole-body uptake of a substance to flow multiplied by the difference between inflowing and outflowing concentration. The boundary and steady-state assumptions must match the application.
required_concepts: Substance uptake equals flow times the appropriate concentration difference.
major_error_concepts: Using arterial and venous partial pressures as if they were automatically total oxygen content without conversion.

cards.prompt: What is Fatigue? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fatigue is a task-dependent reduction in the ability to sustain a specified performance, arising through interacting neural, muscular, metabolic, and other factors. It is not universally explained by one metabolite or a single fixed mechanism.
required_concepts: Performance decline depends on task and multiple mechanisms.
major_error_concepts: Attributing all fatigue exclusively to one substance regardless of task and timescale.

cards.prompt: What is Reproductive Endocrinology? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reproductive endocrinology studies hormonal coordination of reproductive development, gamete production, and reproductive cycles. Feedback and life stage shape these processes, so one isolated hormone concentration cannot fully describe reproductive function.
required_concepts: Hormonal networks coordinate stage-dependent reproductive processes.
major_error_concepts: Inferring complete reproductive function from one hormone value without timing or context.

cards.prompt: What is Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis links regulatory signals with gonadal hormone production and gametogenesis through feedback. Signal timing and pulsatility can matter as well as average concentration.
required_concepts: A timed feedback network coordinates gonadal function.
major_error_concepts: Assuming continuous and pulsatile signals always produce identical downstream responses.

cards.prompt: What is Gametogenesis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gametogenesis produces and matures reproductive cells through coordinated cellular and developmental processes. Meiosis reduces chromosome-set number in the standard sexual cycle, while maturation and supportive tissue functions differ between reproductive systems.
required_concepts: Gamete formation integrates meiosis with specialized maturation.
major_error_concepts: Equating gametogenesis solely with one mitotic division that preserves diploidy in the gamete.

cards.prompt: What is Reproductive Cycles? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reproductive cycles coordinate changes in endocrine signals and target tissues over time. Ovarian and uterine events are linked but distinct, and timing varies rather than every individual following one exact textbook schedule.
required_concepts: Coupled endocrine and tissue cycles have variable timing.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a fixed day-by-day schedule applies exactly to every person and cycle.

cards.prompt: What is Fertilization and Implantation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Fertilization combines gamete contributions to form a zygote, while implantation establishes interaction of an early embryo with uterine tissue in typical mammalian development. These are distinct events separated by intervening development.
required_concepts: Gamete fusion differs from later embryo-tissue establishment.
major_error_concepts: Treating fertilization and implantation as the same immediate event.

cards.prompt: What is Lactation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Lactation involves production and delivery of milk through coordinated mammary, hormonal, and neural processes. Milk synthesis and milk ejection are distinct functions, and demand-related feedback contributes to regulation.
required_concepts: Production and ejection use coordinated but different mechanisms.
major_error_concepts: Equating the signal for milk ejection with all mechanisms of milk synthesis.

cards.prompt: What is Circadian Rhythm? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Circadian rhythms are approximately daily biological oscillations generated by internal timing systems and adjusted by environmental cues. They are not merely passive responses to light, and different rhythms can be shifted relative to one another.
required_concepts: Endogenous timing interacts with external entrainment cues.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a circadian rhythm stops existing whenever light is absent.

cards.prompt: What is Sleep Regulation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sleep involves organized changes in neural and physiological state rather than complete shutdown of brain activity. Sleep stages and regulation interact with circadian timing and prior wakefulness, so duration alone does not describe every aspect of sleep physiology.
required_concepts: Active state regulation includes multiple stages and timing influences.
major_error_concepts: Defining sleep as a period when the brain has no activity.

cards.prompt: What is Stress Physiology? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Physiological stress responses coordinate neural, endocrine, and metabolic adjustments to perceived or actual demands. Effects depend on duration, controllability, and context, so acute adaptive responses and persistent dysregulation should not be treated as identical.
required_concepts: Demand responses vary with timing and context.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every stress response is inherently harmful or every prolonged response is harmless adaptation.

cards.prompt: What is Physiological Aging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Physiological aging involves changes in functional reserve, regulation, and tissue properties over time. Variation among individuals and systems is substantial, and age-associated change is not equivalent to one inevitable disease or uniform loss in every function.
required_concepts: Time-associated changes differ across people and physiological systems.
major_error_concepts: Assuming chronological age uniquely determines every organ's functional capacity.

cards.prompt: What is Physiological Measurement? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Physiological measurement requires a defined variable, method, boundary, and time context. Concentration, flow, content, capacity, and response are different quantities, so a valid measurement supports only claims appropriate to its scope.
required_concepts: Measurement definitions and context constrain physiological inference.
major_error_concepts: Using one concentration as a direct substitute for flow, total content, and functional capacity simultaneously.

cards.prompt: What is Integrated Physiology? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Integrated physiology explains how systems coordinate to meet demands while maintaining viable internal conditions. Compensation can preserve one variable at a cost elsewhere, so apparently normal values do not imply every underlying process is unchanged.
required_concepts: Interacting control systems produce tradeoffs and compensated states.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one normal regulated value proves complete normality of every contributing system.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Physiology.
